hook.text: Here's a trained logistic regression, all of it: eleven numbers. And here's a trained nearest-neighbours model: every one of its hundred and sixty training rows.

hook-why.text: Squeezing the data into a fixed set of numbers, or keeping it, decides how a model learns, what it costs to serve, and how it fails.

plan.text: Eighteen questions: thirteen worked through, then five quick ones.

gd-in.text: First, how the numbers are found.

gd.text: Question one. How does gradient descent work? The gradient of the loss points uphill, so step each weight the other way, scaled by the learning rate, and repeat.

gd-run.text: The page's run: a hundred noisy rows made from three weights, one, two and minus one. From zero, five hundred steps at a rate of point oh one reach point nine nine, one point nine three and minus point nine four: close, and still moving.

batch.text: Question two. What's the difference between batch gradient descent, SGD, and mini-batch GD? How many rows each step averages.

batch-each.text: Batch uses all of them: an exact gradient and a smooth path, but every step reads the whole dataset. Stochastic gradient descent, SGD, uses one row: cheap, noisy steps that can shake loose from a shallow minimum, but never quite settle.

batch-mini.text: Mini-batch, typically thirty-two to five hundred and twelve rows, is the default: less noise, and one matrix multiply that keeps the hardware busy.

batch-run.text: Thirty steps each: batch's path is smooth, and reads three thousand rows. Single rows wander, get about as far, and read thirty.

lr.text: Question three. How do you choose the learning rate, and how do you schedule it?

lr-band.text: Too small and training crawls: the page's point oh one needs nearly twelve hundred steps to settle. Too large and each step overshoots, so the loss climbs, here past about two. At point nine, it settles in nine.

lr-range.text: A real network's limit is unknown, so run a range test: one short run with the rate rising across orders of magnitude.

lr-sched.text: Then schedule it: a short warmup, because early updates are large and unstable, then decay toward zero, so noisy steps can settle. Single-row SGD at a constant rate ends about point oh three from the best answer; decayed on a cosine, about point oh oh one.

lr-adam.text: Adaptive optimizers like Adam scale each weight's step, but the base rate still needs tuning.

logit-in.text: Now one model, and the loss it learns from.

logit.text: Question four. How does logistic regression work? It weights the features into a score, the log odds, and the sigmoid squeezes that into a probability. Training minimizes binary cross-entropy, or log loss.

logit-run.text: On the page's data, it scores seventy-five percent on forty held-out rows, with probabilities like point nine six and point one nine.

logit-prod.text: It's a classifier despite its name, and a strong baseline: one dot product to serve, weights you can read, and a threshold set separately, from the cost of each error.

ce.text: Question five. What is cross-entropy loss, and why is it preferred over MSE for classification? It's minus the log of the probability given to the true class, so a confident wrong answer costs without limit.

ce-grad.text: Behind a sigmoid, squared error's gradient is multiplied by the sigmoid's slope, which is nearly zero exactly when the model is confidently wrong. Cross-entropy's gradient is just the error.

ce-run.text: Start the page's model confidently wrong, right on fourteen percent of rows. Cross-entropy reaches eighty-five percent in twenty-four steps. Squared error, at the same rate, takes two hundred and thirty-four.

param-in.text: That model kept eleven numbers. Not every model keeps a summary.

param.text: Question six. What's the difference between a parametric and a non-parametric model? Parametric models learn a fixed set of numbers and predict from those alone, like linear models and neural networks. Non-parametric ones use the training data to predict, and grow with it, like kNN or a kernel SVM.

param-cost.text: That's a serving decision. At ten million rows, the logistic model is still eleven numbers. Nearest neighbours keeps all ten million, and checks every one for each prediction.

knn.text: Question seven. How does k-nearest neighbours, kNN, work? It finds the k training rows closest to a new point, usually by straight-line distance, and takes their majority class, or their mean. Here, fifteen neighbours vote eleven to four.

knn-trade.text: There's no training step, but inference is slow, and in high dimensions every point ends up about equally far away. Pick k by cross-validation. At scale, approximate nearest-neighbour indexes trade a little accuracy for a lot of speed.

svm.text: Question eight. How does a support vector machine, an SVM, work? It finds the boundary with the widest margin between the classes. The points on or inside the margin are the support vectors, and they alone fix it.

svm-kernel.text: The kernel trick bends that boundary without building new features. On two noisy rings, a straight boundary scores fifty-four percent; a radial basis function kernel, eighty-nine.

svm-cost.text: The follow-up is cost. Where classes overlap, many rows become support vectors, here five thousand three hundred of twenty thousand, and every prediction checks them all. Doubling the rows more than tripled the fit time, measured once in the browser's Python.

scale-in.text: Distances, margins and gradients all take a feature's units at face value.

scale.text: Question nine. What is feature scaling, and why does it matter? It puts features on comparable ranges, by standardizing or min-max scaling. Simulate customers whose age, in years, and income, in dollars, matter equally.

scale-knn.text: Unscaled, kNN scores seventy-four and a half percent, exactly what income alone scores: in raw distance, the whole span of ages counts for no more than fifty dollars. Standardized, eighty-nine.

scale-gd.text: Multiply one of the page's columns by a hundred, as if dollars became cents, and gradient descent goes from eight steps to nearly eighty thousand.

scale-prod.text: Distance models, regularized models and gradient training need it; trees don't. And fit the scaler on training data only, then ship it with the model.

pca.text: Question ten. What is PCA, and what does it do? Principal component analysis finds the directions of greatest variance, each at right angles to those before, and projects the data onto the first few, to compress, plot or decorrelate it.

pca-run.text: On the page's ten scaled features, two components keep forty-two percent of the variance, and the last two keep none: two of the columns are combinations of others.

pca-trap.text: The trap is that variance isn't signal. In this simulation, the first component holds ninety-seven percent of the variance, and predicts the label barely better than a coin flip. The other three percent predicts it at ninety-one. PCA never sees the label.

bag-in.text: One model only goes so far. Next, many.

bag.text: Question eleven. What are ensembles? Explain bagging and boosting. Bagging trains models independently, each on a bootstrap sample, and averages them, mainly cutting variance. Boosting trains them in sequence, each correcting the last, mainly cutting bias, and it overfits unless regularized.

bag-floor.text: Averaging has a floor: adding models cuts the variance only down to a level set by how correlated their errors are.

forest.text: Question twelve. How does a random forest differ from a single decision tree? It bags trees, and at each split lets a tree consider only a random few features: here, eight of the sixty-four pixels of handwritten digits.

forest-run.text: One tree scores eighty-four percent. Each forest tree is weaker than a plain bagged tree, seventy-six percent against eighty-two, but their mistakes overlap less, so together they score ninety-eight against ninety-six.

gb.text: Question thirteen. What is gradient boosting? It adds shallow trees one at a time, each fitted to the negative gradient of the loss: for squared error, the residuals. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost add sampling, L one and L two penalties, and histogram splits for speed.
gb.spoken: Question thirteen. What is gradient boosting? It adds shallow trees one at a time, each fitted to the negative gradient of the loss: for squared error, the residuals. Ex-gee-boost, LightGBM and CatBoost add sampling, L one and L two penalties, and histogram splits for speed.

gb-rate.text: The follow-up is how many trees. On a synthetic benchmark, with each tree scaled by a learning rate of one, validation error is lowest after twelve trees, then climbs. At point one, it keeps falling until seven hundred and eighty-four, to less than half the error.

gb-prod.text: Early stopping on validation picks the count, and every tree runs again for each prediction, so the count is also a latency budget.

r-types.text: Supervised learning maps inputs to labels. Unsupervised finds structure without them, as in clustering. Reinforcement learning has an agent learn by trial and error, maximizing reward.

r-loss.text: For regression, MSE, or MAE for robustness to outliers, or Huber, which blends them. For classification, binary cross-entropy, or categorical cross-entropy with softmax. For ranking, hinge, contrastive or triplet loss.

r-kmeans.text: k-means assigns each point to the nearest centroid, moves each centroid to its points' mean, and repeats to a local minimum, so run several starts, and pick k by the elbow or the silhouette. It assumes round clusters: on stretched ones, about one point in five lands wrong.

r-onehot.text: One-hot encoding gives each category its own column of zeros and ones, implying no order: red, green and blue become three columns. Set to ignore unknowns, it encodes purple, unseen in training, as all zeros, not an error at serving time. For thousands of values, use hashing or embeddings.

r-fe.text: Feature engineering turns raw data into useful inputs: interactions, the hour or weekday, logs of skewed values, bins, rolling aggregates. Good features often matter more than the algorithm.

next.text: Each of these is a few lines of NumPy, and the coding round asks you to write them, fast and safely. Next: coding for machine learning.

lr-range-read.text: Here the loss bottoms out from about point five, and turns up at two.

lr-range-pick.text: Pick a rate where it's still falling steeply, about a tenth of where it turns up.
